question: What two channels does Document 1 say spread the 2008 U.S. crisis worldwide, and how does Document 3 describe China's experience of the slowdown?
answer: Document 1 identifies two channels for the global spread of the 2008 U.S. crisis: trade and financial. Document 3 notes that China experienced a slowdown in growth but saw its registered urban unemployment rate remain stable.
cited_text:
[DOC1:p2] One might have hoped that the crisis would remain largely contained in the United States. As Table 1-1 and Figure 1-1 both show, this was not the case. The U.S. crisis quickly became a world crisis. Other countries were affected through two chan- nels. The first channel was trade. As U.S. consumers and firms cut spending, part of the decrease fell on imports of foreign goods. Looking at it from the viewpoint of countries exporting to the United States, their exports went down, and so, in turn, did their out- put. The second channel was financial. U.S. banks, badly needing funds in the United States, repatriated funds from other countries, creating problems for banks in those countries as well. The result was not just a U.S. but a world recession. By 2009, average growth in advanced economies was -3.7%, by far the lowest annual growth rate since the Great Depression. Growth in emerging and developing economies remained posi- tive but was nearly 4 percentage points lower than the 2000–2007 average.

[DOC3:p1] Contents: B.1 Okun's law revisited; B.2 Two ways of measuring inflation; B.3 U.S. labour market indicators; B.4 China: slower growth, stable unemployment; Erratum; Appendix C Unverified reader commentary. Key messages 1. Okun's law has held up well through the crisis: adding 2011-2013 barely changes the estimated slope. 2. Headline CPI inflation is far more volatile than either the GDP deflator or core CPI, mostly because of energy prices. In 2009 the gap between headline and core CPI inflation was unusually large. 3. Participation in the U.S. labour force fell during the crisis, so the unemployment rate understates the weakness of the labour market. 4. China's growth has slowed, but its registered urban unemployment rate has not moved. DOC3 | Briefing B: Labour Markets, Prices and Policy Trade-offs Page 1
